titre: The First Iguanodon Wore a Horn That Never Existed
accroche: For lack of a complete skeleton, the first Iguanodon wore a spike on its nose for fifty years, before thirty Belgian skeletons put it back on the thumb.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1825, the English country doctor Gideon Mantell publishes, in the Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, the description of a fossil reptile he names Iguanodon, based on teeth found in the quarries of Tilgate Forest, in Sussex. He has only fragments: teeth, a few scattered bones, nothing that would allow a whole skeleton to be reconstructed. Among these fragments is a pointed, curved bone, and no one knows where it attached to the animal's body.

## A Spike Placed on the Nose

Mantell chooses to set this bone as a horn at the tip of the snout, in his first reconstructions. The idea spreads widely when the sculptor Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins turns it into life-size statues for the Crystal Palace in London, inaugurated in 1854: stocky, four-legged beasts, with a rhinoceros horn planted on the nose. These sculptures, still visible today at Sydenham, become the first public image of a dinosaur ever shown on a large scale, and fix the horn in the imagination for an entire generation.

## Thirty Skeletons Find Their Thumb

The correction comes from an unexpected strike of the pickaxe. In late March 1878, Belgian miners digging a coal shaft at Bernissart, 322 meters underground, come across bones. Over the next three years, about thirty Iguanodon skeletons are extracted, several of them nearly complete, a flood of material compared with the handful of fragments Mantell had half a century earlier. The Belgian paleontologist Louis Dollo supervises their study and mounting: on whole skeletons, the pointed bone systematically occupies the same place, at the end of the hand, in the position of the thumb. No nasal horn: a bony spike at the tip of the thumb, a weapon or a tool, attached to a forelimb and not to a skull.

## What a Fragment Cannot Say on Its Own

The episode is not a case of blindness on Mantell's part: from isolated teeth and bones, with no anatomical landmark to locate them, the horn hypothesis was reasonable, and nothing in the fragments available in 1825 made it possible to choose between it and a competing hypothesis. The correction came neither from finer reasoning nor from a better theory, but from a quantity of material that no paleontologist had yet had in hand: thirty complete individuals, found all at once, instead of a single, incomplete one. An isolated fragment always carries several possible stories; it takes several, assembled, for anatomy to decide.

repere.texte: Thirty Iguanodon skeletons, several of them nearly complete, are extracted between 1878 and 1881 from a coal shaft at Bernissart, at a depth of 322 meters, fifty-three years after Gideon Mantell's first description of the animal from mere fragments.
repere.source: Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences

carte.punch: The first reconstructed Iguanodon had a horn on its nose. It was its thumb.
carte.idee: In 1825, for lack of a complete skeleton, Gideon Mantell places a pointed bone as a horn on the Iguanodon's nose. The error lasts fifty-three years, until the thirty or so Bernissart skeletons (1878): the bone is always in the same place, at the tip of the thumb, not on the skull.
carte.source_courte: Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Full timeline of the discovery, the successive reconstructions and the role of Louis Dollo.

quiz.question: Why was the real position of the Iguanodon's bony spike established only in 1878, more than fifty years after its discovery?
choix: Because it took the discovery of thirty complete skeletons at Bernissart to see this bone always in the same place, on the hand
Because Mantell refused to reconsider his first hypothesis out of pride
Because fossil dating techniques did not yet exist in 1825
Because the bony spike took fifty years to be physically found in the English quarries
quiz.explication: Nothing suggests a stubborn refusal on Mantell's part: with mere fragments, a nasal horn was a reasonable hypothesis, impossible to distinguish from another without more material. Dating has nothing to do with the position of a bone on a skeleton. It is the unprecedented quantity of complete skeletons found at Bernissart that made it possible to see, this time, where this bone was systematically located.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where does Gideon Mantell find the fragments he uses to describe Iguanodon in 1825?
choix: In the quarries of Tilgate Forest, in Sussex, England
In a coal shaft near Bernissart, Belgium
On the cliffs of Dover, at the border with France
In a cave in the Pyrenees, during a dig funded by the Royal Society
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Mantell describes Iguanodon in 1825 from teeth and scattered bones found in the quarries of Tilgate Forest, in Sussex, without any complete skeleton.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does the horn imagined by Mantell spread widely in the public imagination, before the Bernissart discovery?
choix: Through a series of British stamps issued in 1840
Through a popular children's novel published in 1830, largely inspired by Mantell's work
Through the statues by the sculptor Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins, inaugurated at the Crystal Palace in 1854
Through lectures given by Mantell himself at the Royal Society
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The life-size statues sculpted by Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins for the Crystal Palace, inaugurated in 1854 and still visible at Sydenham, widely spread the image of an Iguanodon with a nasal horn.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How many Iguanodon skeletons are extracted from the Bernissart coal shaft between 1878 and 1881, and who supervises their study?
choix: About ten skeletons, studied by Gideon Mantell in person
About thirty skeletons, several of them nearly complete, studied by Louis Dollo
Only two complete skeletons, studied by Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins
About a hundred scattered fragments, with no complete skeleton, studied by the Royal Society
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Between 1878 and 1881, about thirty skeletons, several of them nearly complete, are extracted from the Bernissart shaft; the Belgian paleontologist Louis Dollo supervises their study and mounting.
